title: Locked Out or Broken In?
summary: One alert: a string of failed sign-ins, then a successful one. Someone guessing a password - or just a person with an old password saved? Read the SIEM and decide.
story: You are the analyst on shift in {{CO}}'s small security team (a made-up company). The SIEM - the system that collects every computer's logs in one place - raised an alert a few minutes ago: many failed sign-ins for one account, followed by a sign-in that worked. Your job is not to panic and not to ignore it: look at the events behind the alert and decide whether it is a real attack or a false alarm.
goal: Decide whether the alert is real, and answer the questions about it: the account, where the failed sign-ins came from, which computer they were aimed at, how many there were, and when they started.
skills: reading SIEM alerts, Windows sign-in events (4624, 4625), searching and counting events

guess.WHY: The failed sign-ins came from an address outside the company, over remote desktop, and ended in a successful sign-in from that same address: someone guessed the password.

stale.WHY: The failed sign-ins came from the person's own computer, minutes after they changed their password, over the network to the file server: an old password still saved on that computer. Once they updated it, the sign-in worked.

questions.ask: Is this alert a real attack or a false alarm? (real / false alarm - you get one try)
Which account had the failed sign-ins?
questions.explain: The alert and every 4625 event name it.

questions.ask: Which address did the failed sign-ins come from?
questions.explain: The src_ip field of the 4625 events.

questions.ask: Which computer were the sign-ins aimed at (the host that logged them)?
questions.explain: The host field of the 4625 events.

questions.ask: How many failed sign-ins were there for that account?
questions.explain: siem search source=winsec event=4625 user={{U}} counts them.

questions.ask: At what time (HH:MM:SS) was the first failed sign-in?
questions.explain: The events are listed oldest first; the first 4625 is at {{T0}}.

hints.text: What to think about first: an alert is only a starting point - a rule in the SIEM noticed a pattern. Your job is to look at the events behind it and ask: who, from where, to where, how many, and does it make sense? Failed sign-ins happen all the time (people mistype), so the details decide whether it is an attack.

Type siem alerts to see the alert. Then look at the sign-in events: siem search source=winsec event=4625 shows every failed sign-in (4625 is Windows' number for 'a sign-in failed'; 4624 means it worked). Each line has fields like user=, src_ip= (where it came from) and host= (the computer that wrote it down).

To count, narrow the search to the account and read the last line, which says how many events matched: siem search source=winsec event=4625 user=NAME. The results are in time order, so the first line is the first failed sign-in. siem search source=winsec user=NAME shows the successful one (4624) too.

Deciding: addresses starting like the company's own computers (the same first three numbers as the WS- computers in the SIEM) are inside the building. An address from outside, logon_type=10 (remote desktop) and a sign-in that finally works from that same address is someone guessing a password. Failures from the person's own computer to a file server right after they changed their password (event 4723) is an old saved password - annoying, not an attack.
